headline: Over $100M in data center gear hijacked in transit by organized crime since June 2026
summary: Organized crime syndicates are intercepting data center shipments, using hacking, phishing, and even vehicular ramming. These sophisticated heists net tens of millions per shipment, with over $100 million stolen since June 2026.
details: Organized crime teams are hijacking data center gear in transit, with over $100 million worth of computing and related equipment stolen since June 2026 alone. These sophisticated operations can net tens of millions of dollars per single shipment.

The trend has been growing, with notable incidents including a $38 million gear disappearance in Reno this year. Other major thefts include $15 million in semiconductors and Apple products in Reno in July 2025, and $13 million in gear around the Mojave Desert in June 2026.

Stolen items range from servers, fiber-optic and copper cabling, RAM modules, and drives, to routers and other miscellaneous components. Even copper wire is highly valued, with one snagged trailer containing $300,000 worth of the metal.

Thieves employ a mix of technological and brutal methods. They gain access to online accounts of freight brokers and carriers, allowing them to view cargo manifests, shipping schedules, and impersonate shipping companies.

Physical tactics include tracking shipments, issuing false ones, and even vehicular ramming of escort cars to facilitate a getaway. Some heists suggest truck drivers may be complicit, potentially recruited using AI-generated IDs and poor vetting.

To counter tracking, malfeasants have used GPS beacon impersonation, broadcasting fake coordinates to mislead both human and automated systems. This ensures the stolen cargo's location remains undetected.

The stolen gear often has overseas buyers lined up before the heist, with law enforcement believing the equipment is acquired by entities in countries under tight U.S. AI export controls, such as China. Suspicious activity has also been linked to India, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Colombia, and Moldova.

Supply management experts describe these operations as international syndicates that function like large corporations. They have infiltrated supply chains at all levels, from drivers to warehouse operators, identifying weak points for exploitation.

headline: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt financing for GPUs expected in H1 2027, Musk says
summary: The GPUs are expected to arrive in the first half of 2027. This massive investment is backed by SpaceX's investment-grade status and revenue from Starlink and space businesses.
details: SpaceX has secured $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units (GPUs), a deal confirmed by Elon Musk. These high-performance chips are anticipated to arrive in the first half of 2027.

Musk disclosed the deal on X, explaining that SpaceX was able to secure this funding due to its investment-grade status and substantial revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and space businesses. This positions the company uniquely compared to many competitors without independent AI-related revenue.

The announcement came in response to investor concerns about mounting financing pressures and potential delays in data center construction impacting AI computing capacity. Musk agreed that many smaller "neoclouds" would likely face consolidation as debt markets have largely shut off funding for companies without substantial revenue outside of AI data centers.

While Musk confirmed the financing has "closed," it remains unclear what this entails regarding final debt pricing or investor agreements. This significant investment aligns with SpaceX's projected capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion in Q4, as stated by CFO Bret Johnsen.

Earlier reports indicated a proposed $40 billion debt package for Nvidia hardware, potentially covering around 360,000 Rubin GPUs across 5,000 Nvidia NVL72 racks. Musk has not yet confirmed the specific GPU models or quantities covered by the now-closed deal.

This massive spending fits into Musk's broader strategy to significantly expand AI computing capacity. xAI, another Musk company, outlined plans in August to increase its data center capacity sevenfold by 2027, targeting 10 gigawatts. SpaceXAI also reportedly aims to add another 660,000 Nvidia GPUs during 2026, potentially bringing its total to 1.44 million.

Beyond just GPUs, data centers require substantial investment in power, cooling, networking equipment, and physical infrastructure. SpaceX has also begun selling access to its own infrastructure, including deals with Anthropic for its Colossus 1 supercomputer and Google for approximately 110,000 Nvidia GPUs.
